Asanoha Spherical Kumiko Shell is a true 360° sculpture: the traditional Asanoha (麻の葉) star lattice is grown as a triple-scale fractal directly on a perfect sphere (no “front/back”). 

The pattern is mapped via a dual Lambert azimuthal equal-area projection: one star core anchors the north pole, one anchors the south pole, with a seamless ±15° equatorial blend. 

Relief is created by radial displacement along surface normals (0.0–0.9, up to 30% of radius), forming structural ribs and deep shadow valleys. 

A PAPP substrate (S³ sampling + Hopf modulation) subtly tunes ridge sharpness and flow.

Mesh: 57,122 verts / 114,240 faces, closed manifold (χ=2), per-vertex color

Tech: wallpaper group p6m; triple-scale s=0.850/0.525/0.325; canyon_depth=0.5; seed [6,12,60,16]→β=23.5→CF[23,2]→(p,q)=(2,23)→triple(525,92,533)→V4d=2529*; edges 171,360; vertex colors 32,149; r=3.0–3.9.

192681f6be9e443f86c48aaf13b8833b.name: Bark Midge - insect
192681f6be9e443f86c48aaf13b8833b.description: The Bark Midge (Corticomyia lignivora) is a sap-feeding insect commonly found in temperate forests. Its mottled brown exoskeleton mimics tree bark, providing excellent camouflage against predators. Measuring about 8mm long, it has large, dark compound eyes for detecting movement and short, sensitive antennae. Its slender legs end in tiny claws that allow it to cling to tree trunks and branches with ease. Unlike mosquitoes, Bark Midges do not bite; instead, they use specialized mouthparts to pierce tree bark and feed on sap, playing a role in nutrient cycling. Their delicate, translucent wings have subtle speckling that helps them blend into dappled light. These insects are most active at dawn and dusk, avoiding direct sunlight. Bark Midges are an essential part of the forest ecosystem, providing food for birds, spiders, and amphibians. Though rarely noticed due to their excellent camouflage, they are widespread across North America and Europe, quietly contributing to the health of their woodland habitats.
